prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks, creating credit cycles
for methods to estimate demand and dynamic competition in differentiated-product industries

statement.case_for: Both parts rest on one common test: a discovery with a clear origin, durable use across fields, and years of confirmation. Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is a single mechanism with unambiguous two-author credit. Collateral values and borrowing limits feed back on each other, so small shocks become large and persistent. The mechanism became a basic component of macro-finance and of post-2008 policy modelling, and the amplification channel is now standard in theory and quantitative work. Pakes's programme (random-coefficients demand estimation with Berry and Levinsohn, the Ericson-Pakes dynamic framework, and the productivity-estimation methods developed with Olley) made structural empirical industrial organisation workable. It has been used for about three decades in merger review, regulation, trade and other applied fields, so the maturity concern is small. Setting them side by side, the first part is a mechanism and the second is an estimation framework. Together they would cover both conceptual and methodological contributions, and neither is a recent or provisional result. Dropping Gertler from my opening trio is deliberate. The two-name credit for B002 is cleaner, and it frees one slot under the three-person cap for the B012 anchor.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution in B012. The demand-side breakthrough is Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes (1995), and crediting Pakes alone leaves out Berry and Levinsohn. It also leaves out Bresnahan and Reiss, who laid earlier empirical-IO foundations. The three-person cap forces this, and the citation has to rest on Pakes's wider programme rather than on one paper. A second concern is that a prize pairing macro-finance with empirical IO has no obvious shared theme, and the Committee may prefer a single focused achievement. For B002, the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises is adjacent, and empirical identification of the collateral amplification channel is less clean than the theory. If the Committee rejects Pakes-alone, B002 with Gertler as a single-part trio would be my fallback.

responses.point: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is the core of B002. The financial accelerator is a distinct strand of Bernanke, Gertler and Gilchrist, and Bernanke's 2022 prize complicates adding Gertler or Gilchrist.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution core and have moved toward your view. My opening trio included Gertler, but the accelerator is a different mechanism from collateral-driven credit cycles, and a citation covering both would blur the discovery. I am not certain the 2022 prize actually covers the accelerator, since it was awarded for work on banks and financial crises. The overlap is a risk for the Committee to weigh, not a settled fact. The cap also has an opportunity cost, because a third name for Gertler displaces a name elsewhere. On that basis I confine B002 to Kiyotaki and Moore.

responses.point: Gertler belongs in the B002 trio for the financial-accelerator and macro-financial strand, with the award centred on the collateral-constraint and credit-cycle contribution. Hassler also flags that the credit division between the two strands is contestable.
responses.response: I opened with the same trio, so I take the argument seriously. The difficulty is that Gertler's most influential work is the Bernanke-Gertler lineage, and he also appears among the eight names in B043. That makes his credit divided between two ballot entries. Under common criteria the clearest identifiable origin should carry the citation, and that is Kiyotaki-Moore. I would reopen the question if the Committee wants a broader financial-frictions citation. The inclusion of Gertler then depends on how it is framed, and I do not think the evidence settles it.

responses.point: Pakes is the central figure of B012 through BLP, Ericson-Pakes and estimation methods. A three-person prize anchored on Pakes with the BLP core is the cleanest, while Bresnahan and others are more separable.
responses.response: Your argument for Pakes as the anchor is what lets me credit him alone. His contributions cover demand estimation, dynamic games and productivity estimation, so a single-laureate citation on methods for demand and dynamic competition is defensible. I disagree only on cost. Berry and Levinsohn are not peripheral to BLP, and omitting them is a real attribution loss that I want on the record. I accept it only because the three-person cap binds in a two-part configuration.

responses.point: B050 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) built a formal, empirically testable framework for how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy. He also notes the possible overlap with the 2024 institutions prize and that some causal claims about electoral rules are contested.
responses.response: I agree B050 is a coherent field-creating contribution, and I keep it as an alternative. I qualify one point. The contested causal claims you mention carry weight under common criteria, because cross-country constitutional comparisons often cannot rule out reverse causality. The mechanism and the credit are cleaner in B002 and the methods in B012 are better confirmed. The 2024 adjacency matters mainly for timing and balance. I do not treat it as a scientific demerit. My field is adjacent to this area, so I discount any affinity I feel for it.

uncertainties: Whether crediting Pakes alone is acceptable given Berry and Levinsohn's role in BLP and the exclusion of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin.
Whether the Committee prefers a single focused B002 award, possibly with Gertler, over a two-part configuration spanning macro-finance and empirical IO.
How much of the collateral-constraint mechanism the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises already covers.
How strong the empirical identification of collateral-driven amplification is relative to the theory.
Whether the structural assumptions behind BLP-type estimation are robust enough, given continuing identification debates.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the preferred parts B002 and B012. The profile lists no collaborator among their credited names. For the alternative B050, my field (comparative political institutions) is adjacent. The profile also lists a co-author named only 'Persson' (corruption as a collective-action problem, with Rothstein). It does not give a first name or link that person to Torsten Persson. My opening note identifying him as Torsten Persson is therefore not supported by the supplied profile and should be treated as unverified. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it.
